# LITs with `tags` `philosophy-of-technology`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Philosophy of technology** — what technology is and what it does to those who live with it — the autonomy of technique, technological determinism and the social shaping of technology, lock-in and practical compulsion, automation and deskilling, technical codes and the politics of artifacts, design that steers or captures its users, critical theory of technology and convivial tools. A technology's regulation stays with society-and-governance, a measured effect of one product with social-science and a verdict on what is owed with ethics, unless the work argues about technology as such; how software is built is software-engineering (group: philosophy; ADR-098).

| [LIT-731](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-731.md) v2 | Tiktok's enshittification | Doctorow (2023), Pluralistic, 21 January. Platforms die in three stages: good to users, then abusing users for business customers, then abusing both to take the value for themselves. It follows from the ease of reallocating value in a two-sided market, and lock-in, blocked interoperability and monopoly sustain it. TikTok's "heating" of chosen creators is read as stage two beginning. Remedy: end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-573.md)): in full, from the author's own blog, under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Worth reading as the essay that named enshittification and the earliest statement of it the record holds. Platforms are first good to users, then abuse users for business customers, then abuse both to claw back value; each stage is made possible by the lock-in the last one built, and blocked interoperability raises how much abuse users will bear before leaving. The remedy proposed is end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. Limits: an opinion essay argued from cases, with linked journalism and the author's own experience as evidence; its TikTok claim is a prediction. |

| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) v2 | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |

| [LIT-897](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-897.md) v3 | AI as Agency without Intelligence: On Artificial Intelligence as a New Form of Artificial Agency and the Multiple Realisability of Agency Thesis | Floridi (2025), DOI-10.1007/s13347-025-00858-9. Read it as a taxonomy, not an argument. The case for MRA over ARI is announced and not made, since the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind. AI's lack of intelligence is asserted. | [LIT-1002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1002.md) v4 | Technology, autonomy, and manipulation | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum (2019), Internet Policy Review 8(2). Manipulation is hidden influence: intentionally and covertly influencing someone's decision-making by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities, where covert means the target is not and could not easily become aware of it. Surveillance, adaptive interfaces and the habitual invisibility of technology make it easy. Its harm is to autonomy, in both competency and authenticity, and beneficent manipulation carries it too; the paper claims a harm in every case, not that manipulation is always wrong. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md)) in full; worth reading for the standard statement of the covert-influence view: manipulation is "intentionally and covertly influencing their decision-making, by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities", with attempted covertness as its mark, and for the argument that its harm is to autonomy and is carried even by beneficent manipulation, through the target's opacity to herself. Read it knowing that it is a short policy essay, that the definition is stipulated and its intent requirement never examined, that it excludes manipulation of institutions and never considers manipulation by them, and that it claims a harm in every case, not a wrong. |
| [LIT-1297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1297.md) v2 | The End of Ownership: Personal Property in the Digital Economy | Perzanowski and Schultz (2016). Digital media and software-laden devices are sold under licences that deny a sale and DRM that enforces the licence, while the law of exhaustion, built around owning a tangible copy, cannot follow purchases that are copied at every use or never copied at all. Buyers lose resale, lending, repair and privacy, and a survey shows "Buy Now" misleads them. The book proposes treating one-time purchases as sales, judging licences as permissions rather than contracts, exempting owners from anti-circumvention law, and a multifactor test for digital exhaustion. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1026.md)) in full except the last page of the Conclusion, which the copy lacks; worth reading as the standard account of how licences, DRM and the copy-centred law of exhaustion turn digital purchases into conditional access, with the case law from Bobbs-Merrill to Lexmark v. Impression Products, a survey showing that "Buy Now" misleads buyers, and a proposed multifactor test for digital exhaustion. Its diagnosis is the consumer side of Lessig's copy trigger: exhaustion is tied to owning a copy, and digital use and transfer make new copies. Read it knowing that it is US law as of early 2016, that it is advocacy by two authors who were parties or counsel in several of its episodes, that the survey is their own and of a mock store, and that several of its pending cases have since been decided. |

Worth reading for the model that makes lock-in analysable: increasing returns turn the adoption difference into a random walk with absorbing barriers, so one technology takes the market, which one is decided by the order of small events, and the outcome is neither predictable, flexible nor necessarily efficient ([THEORY-863](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-863.md), re-derived). Read it knowing that the model is very special (two types, linear returns, no expectations, pricing or sponsors), that its historical examples are illustrations, and that the published version may differ from the precursor read here. |

| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) v2 | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |

| [LIT-2224](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2224.md) v2 | Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers’ awareness? | Macnamara, Berber, Çavuşoğlu, Krupinski, Nallapareddy, Nelson, Smith, Wilson-Delfosse & Ray (2024). A theoretical perspective, with no data, arguing that AI assistants that take over cognitive work will accelerate skill decay in experts and hinder skill development in learners, outside the performers' awareness. Its premises come from automation research, chiefly aviation: skill decays with disuse, more for cognitive than physical tasks; disuse can be partial, a subtask ceased while the task goes on; in Casner et al.'s pilots, reported second-hand, procedural flying skills held while cognitive skills declined. It separates automation bias and complacency, which end when the automation is removed, from skill loss, which does not, and proposes research questions. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1710.md)) from the CC BY version of record in Europe PMC (PMC11239631); worth reading as a clear statement of how support that does part of a task wears down the operator's skill at that part while the task goes on, and why the loss stays hidden until the support is withdrawn. A theoretical perspective with no data of its own; its aviation evidence, chiefly Casner et al. (2014), is reported second-hand, without samples, sizes or horizons; and its claim that AI assistants accelerate decay beyond automation is a hypothesis it says no research has tested. |

| [LIT-2425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2425.md) v3 | Recommended Selves: Authenticity and Algorithmic Filtering | Brown (2025), DOI-10.1017/apa.2025.10009.
